title: Partition Labels
description: Brute force to optimized: repeatedly searching for last occurrences versus precomputing them once and greedily extending partitions in a single pass.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s, partition it into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part, and return a list of the sizes of these parts. Concatenating the parts in order should reproduce s exactly.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","s, a string of lowercase letters"],["Output","The sizes of the maximal-count partition where each letter stays within one part"],["Goal","Compute this in a single pass using each letter's last occurrence"],["Constraints","1 <= s.length <= 500"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Each letter must stay within one contiguous part\"","Precompute each letter's last occurrence, then greedily extend the current part to cover it"],["\"As many parts as possible\"","Close a part as soon as it is safe to do so (greedy), rather than delaying unnecessarily"]]}

blocks.text: A valid partition boundary can only be placed at a position where every letter seen so far in the current part has ALREADY had its last occurrence. This means tracking, for the current part, the furthest "last occurrence" among all letters seen so far, and closing the part exactly when the current position reaches that boundary.

blocks.title: Analogy: Grouping Guests Who Must All Leave Before the Room Resets
blocks.text: Picture guests entering and leaving a room, where knowing each guest's exact departure time in advance lets you determine the earliest point at which the room could be "reset" (all current guests have left) without splitting any guest's visit across two sessions. This problem asks for the same idea applied to letters in a string.

blocks.caption: Precomputing each letter's last occurrence lets a single pass track when the current partition can safely close

blocks.text: Result: [9, 7, 8]. "ababcbaca" (9 chars), "defegde" (7 chars), "hijhklij" (8 chars) are the 3 maximal parts.

Before trying every possible partition boundary and checking validity, notice that precomputing each letter's LAST occurrence index lets a single left-to-right pass track exactly how far the current partition must extend, closing it the moment the current position catches up to that extent.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Precomputing the last index of every letter in the string (a single pass, O(n)) gives, for any letter, exactly how far right the current partition must reach if that letter appears in it.

Observation 2: Scanning left to right, maintaining a running "end" value as the maximum last-occurrence index among all letters seen SO FAR in the current partition, correctly tracks how far this partition must extend.

Observation 3: The partition can safely close exactly when the current index equals this running "end" value, since at that point, every letter seen in the current partition has had its last occurrence already covered.

Observation 4: Once closed, a new partition starts fresh at the next index, with its own independent running "end" tracking.

This leads to precomputing last occurrences in one pass, then a second pass tracking the running maximum last-occurrence among letters seen so far, closing a partition exactly when the current index reaches that maximum.

Try every possible partition boundary directly, greedily extending the current partition and checking, for each candidate end position, whether any letter inside the current partition also appears later.

items: Starting a new partition at some index, check its ending letters one at a time, extending as needed.
For each candidate end index, verify no letter within the current partition range appears again later in the string.
Once verified safe, close the partition and start the next one.

codes.python:
def partition_labels_brute(s):
    n = len(s)
    result = []
    start = 0
    while start < n:
        end = start
        i = start
        while i <= end:
            last_occurrence = s.rfind(s[i])                 # scan for the last occurrence, repeatedly
            end = max(end, last_occurrence)
            i += 1
        result.append(end - start + 1)
        start = end + 1
    return result

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Repeatedly finding the last occurrence of each letter directly enforces the "no letter spans across a boundary" rule.
Calling rfind/lastIndexOf repeatedly (once per character examined) costs O(n) each time, giving O(n squared) overall.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), repeated last-occurrence scans.
Space: O(1) extra (beyond output).
Limitation: precomputing every letter's last occurrence ONCE upfront (O(n)), rather than searching repeatedly, reduces the total time to O(n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why repeated searching is wasteful: a letter's last occurrence index never changes, so computing it once upfront for every letter (a single O(n) pass) avoids ever re-searching for it.

The precompute-then-scan structure: first pass builds a map from each letter to its last index in s; second pass walks through s, maintaining a running "end" as the maximum last-index among letters seen so far in the current partition.

Closing a partition: exactly when the current index reaches this running "end," since every letter encountered in the current partition has now had its last occurrence accounted for.

The core idea: precompute once, then a single greedy pass tracking and closing partitions based on the running maximum last-occurrence.

Precompute last occurrence indices for every letter in one pass. In a second pass, maintain a running "end" as the max last-occurrence among letters seen so far; close and record a partition whenever the current index equals this "end."

blocks.caption: A running maximum of last-occurrences determines exactly when the current partition can close

codes.python:
def partition_labels(s):
    last = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(s)}           # precompute last occurrence, once
    result = []
    start = end = 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        end = max(end, last[ch])                          # extend to cover this letter's last occurrence
        if i == end:                                        # safe to close here
            result.append(end - start + 1)
            start = i + 1
    return result

blocks.text: Precomputing each letter's last occurrence once means, while scanning left to right, extending the running "end" to the max last-occurrence among letters seen so far correctly represents the furthest point the current partition must reach to safely contain every one of those letters entirely. The moment the current index reaches this "end," it is guaranteed no letter in the current partition appears again later, so closing exactly there is both safe and greedy-optimal (as delaying the close further would only merge in unrelated future letters, producing fewer, larger partitions than necessary).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), two linear passes.
Space: O(1) extra (a fixed-size 26-letter map/array), beyond the output.

blocks.text: Partition Labels is a clean example of "precompute last occurrences, then greedily extend and close partitions," a technique broadly applicable whenever partition boundaries depend on future positions of already-seen elements.

Recomputing last occurrences repeatedly (as in the brute force) instead of precomputing them once upfront.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "partition so each element stays within one part, maximizing partition count", think: precompute each element's last occurrence, then greedily extend and close based on the running maximum.

items: How would you adapt this if elements could repeat with gaps, requiring merging multiple disjoint ranges per letter?

Merge Intervals, since this problem is equivalent to building [first occurrence, last occurrence] intervals per letter and merging overlapping ones.
Any "partition maximally while keeping related elements together" problem, solvable via a running-extent greedy pass.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Repeated last-occurrence searching costs O(n squared) time; precomputing once and scanning greedily costs O(n) time, both using O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: precompute last occurrences once, then a single greedy pass extending and closing partitions.
Core Idea: track a running "end" as the max last-occurrence among letters seen so far; close a partition exactly when the current index reaches it.
Time: O(n squared) for repeated searching, O(n) for the optimized precompute-and-scan approach.
Space: O(1) extra for both, beyond the output.
Most Important Observation: a partition can close exactly when the current position catches up to the furthest last-occurrence among its letters.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, elegant greedy problem connecting to interval merging.
One line memory trick: precompute last occurrences; close a partition when the current index reaches the running max.
